1password.description: 1Password stores your passwords, passkeys, credit cards, and other sensitive items in an encrypted vault you unlock with one master password (plus a secret key), then autofills them across your browser, desktop, and phone. Beyond personal password management it has grown into a broader access-security platform, adding features like a password-health dashboard, SaaS app discovery, device-trust checks, and credential management for AI agents and automated workflows.
1password.name: 1password
1password.pricing_note: individual and family plans, plus separate custom-quoted business/enterprise tiers
requirements: a 1Password account (paid subscription) to store and sync vault data
network access to sync vaults
1password.tagline: The password manager and secrets vault that keeps every login, card, and passkey behind one master password.

1password-beta.description: 1password-beta packages the pre-release beta build of the 1Password desktop app, so users can try new features and fixes before they reach the stable channel. It is the same encrypted password, passkey, and secrets vault as regular 1Password, just built from a newer, less-tested release track.
1password-beta.name: 1password-beta
1password-beta.pricing_note: same 1Password subscription plans as the stable app
requirements: a 1Password account (paid subscription) to store and sync vault data
network access to sync vaults
tolerance for pre-release bugs since this is the beta channel
1password-beta.tagline: The bleeding-edge preview channel of 1Password's password manager, ahead of the stable release.

1password-cli.description: The 1Password CLI (the `op` command) lets you fetch and manage vault items, inject secrets into environment variables, and provision shells with credentials, all without opening the desktop app. It is aimed at developers and admins who want to script secret retrieval, wire secrets into CI pipelines, or manage vaults, users, and service accounts from the command line.
1password-cli.name: 1password-cli
1password-cli.pricing_note: the CLI binary itself is free; it is only useful with a paid 1Password account behind it
requirements: a 1Password account (paid subscription) to authenticate against
network access to reach 1Password's servers
1password-cli.tagline: Read, write, and script your 1Password vault straight from the terminal.

aether.description: Aether analyzes a wallpaper's colors (using a median-cut palette algorithm with several extraction modes and fine-tuning sliders) and generates a cohesive 16-color theme from it, then applies that theme across 20+ apps like Hyprland, Kitty, Alacritty, VS Code, and Neovim. It also bundles a wallpaper browser/downloader for wallhaven.cc, an image editor with filters, and a library of built-in presets (Dracula, Nord, Gruvbox, Catppuccin) plus 250+ importable Base16 community schemes.
aether.name: aether
aether.tagline: Turn any wallpaper into a matching color scheme for your whole Linux desktop.

asdcontrol.description: asdcontrol is a small Linux utility for controlling the brightness of Apple's Thunderbolt-connected displays, specifically the Studio Display and Pro Display XDR. It talks to the monitor over its USB HID interface, letting you read the current brightness or set it to an absolute value or a relative adjustment from a terminal command or a bound hotkey.
asdcontrol.name: asdcontrol
requirements: one of the supported Apple displays (Studio Display 2022, Pro Display XDR) connected via USB-C
read/write access to the display's USB HID device node (usually granted via a udev rule)
asdcontrol.tagline: Command-line brightness control for Apple's Thunderbolt displays, on Linux.

asusctl.description: asusctl is a background daemon plus a set of command-line tools for managing ASUS ROG laptop hardware on Linux: keyboard backlight and per-key RGB lighting, custom fan curves, switching between integrated and dedicated GPU modes, VFIO passthrough toggling for VMs, AniMe Matrix display animations, and power-profile-triggered scripts. A separate companion app, rog-control-center, provides a graphical front end for it, but this package itself is the daemon and CLI layer.
asusctl.name: asusctl
requirements: an ASUS ROG laptop (features vary by model, e.g. AniMe Matrix or per-key RGB only on models that have that hardware)
asusctl.tagline: The control daemon and CLI toolkit that unlocks ASUS ROG laptop features on Linux.

basecamp-cli.description: basecamp-cli is Basecamp's official command-line client, letting you list and manage projects, to-dos, cards, and messages, post updates, and search across your Basecamp account from a terminal. It authenticates via OAuth 2.1 in the browser on first login and then handles token refresh automatically, and it also ships plugins/MCP support so AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Copilot can act on your Basecamp account directly.
basecamp-cli.name: basecamp-cli
basecamp-cli.pricing_note: the CLI is free; it requires a Basecamp account, and Basecamp itself is a paid product
requirements: a Basecamp account
a Basecamp subscription for the underlying project-management service
network access, since it talks to Basecamp's API
basecamp-cli.tagline: Manage your Basecamp projects, to-dos, and messages without leaving the terminal.

bun-bin.description: Bun is an all-in-one JavaScript and TypeScript toolkit: a fast runtime (built in Rust/Zig on JavaScriptCore rather than V8) meant as a drop-in alternative to Node.js, plus a built-in package manager, bundler, and test runner in a single executable. The goal is to collapse a typical JS project's separate tools into one fast binary, cutting install and startup times compared to a traditional Node/npm/webpack/Jest stack.
bun-bin.name: bun-bin
requirements: Linux kernel 5.6+ recommended (5.1 minimum)
bun-bin.tagline: One fast binary that replaces Node.js, npm, webpack, and your test runner.

caja-open-any-terminal.description: This is a Caja (and originally Nautilus) file-manager extension that adds a right-click context-menu entry to open a terminal at the current folder. Rather than being locked to one default terminal, it supports 40+ terminal emulators (Kitty, Alacritty, Konsole, Terminator, and more), configurable through gsettings or a dconf-editor panel.
caja-open-any-terminal.name: caja-open-any-terminal
requirements: a Caja/Nautilus Python extension runtime (nautilus-python or python3-nautilus)
at least one supported terminal emulator installed to open
caja-open-any-terminal.tagline: Adds an "Open Terminal Here" option for your favorite terminal to the Caja file manager.

claude-code.description: Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool: you run it from a project directory and describe what you want in plain language, and it reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and handles git workflows like commits and PRs on your behalf. It runs primarily as a terminal CLI but also integrates with IDEs and GitHub (by tagging @claude on issues or PRs).
claude-code.name: claude-code
claude-code.pricing_note: usable with a Claude.ai subscription (Pro/Max) or pay-as-you-go Anthropic API credits; the official site did not surface exact figures during this review
requirements: a Claude.ai account or Anthropic API key
network access to reach Anthropic's API
claude-code.tagline: An AI coding agent that works directly in your terminal, understands your whole codebase, and ships changes for you.

cliamp.description: cliamp is a retro-styled music player that lives entirely in the terminal, built to evoke Winamp 2.x with a spectrum visualizer and a parametric EQ rendered in ASCII. It plays local files as well as internet radio, podcasts, and streams pulled from YouTube, YouTube Music, SoundCloud, Spotify, Navidrome, Jellyfin, and more. Playlists, a Lua plugin system, and cross-platform support (Linux, macOS, Windows) round it out.
cliamp.name: cliamp
cliamp.pricing_note: MIT licensed, source available on GitHub
requirements: Network access to stream from services like YouTube, Spotify, or internet radio
ffmpeg and yt-dlp needed for extended codec and streaming-provider support
Linux needs ALSA dev headers and a PipeWire-ALSA or PulseAudio-ALSA bridge for audio
cliamp.tagline: Winamp's ghost, reincarnated in your terminal.
cliamp.youtube_title: The Ultimate Terminal Music Player? Meet Cliamp.

crush-bin.description: Crush is a terminal-based AI coding agent from Charm (makers of Bubble Tea and Glow) that works alongside you directly in the command line. It can switch between many LLM providers mid-session without losing context, understands your project through LSP integration, and extends itself through MCP servers over HTTP, stdio, or SSE. Session history and project context are stored locally in SQLite, so nothing is lost between restarts.
crush-bin.name: crush-bin
crush-bin.pricing_note: Source-available under FSL-1.1-MIT (converts to MIT after 2 years); Crush itself costs nothing but you supply your own API key for whichever model provider you use
requirements: An API key from at least one supported LLM provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, Groq, AWS Bedrock, Azure, Vertex AI, or a local model via Ollama/llama.cpp)
Network access to reach the chosen model provider
crush-bin.tagline: Your coding bestie, now living in your favorite terminal.

cursor-bin.description: Cursor is a full desktop coding environment, forked from VS Code, that puts AI agents at the center of the workflow. It lets you pick from multiple frontier models to generate code, run autonomous cloud agents that build and test features in the background, and review pull requests or trigger automations straight from the editor, terminal, or Slack. It's aimed at developers who want an IDE where an AI agent can take on real chunks of implementation work, not just autocomplete.
cursor-bin.name: cursor-bin
cursor-bin.pricing_note: Hobby tier is free with limited agent requests; Pro is $20/mo, Pro+ $60/mo, Ultra $200/mo, Teams from $40/user/mo
requirements: A Cursor account
Network access
A paid plan (Pro or higher) for meaningful agent usage beyond the free tier's limits
cursor-bin.tagline: An AI-first code editor built to build ambitious software.
cursor-bin.youtube_title: Cursor AI: The Only IDE You Need in 2026 (Beginner to Pro)

cursor-cli.description: Cursor CLI brings Cursor's AI coding agents to the terminal, so they can be run interactively, wired into GitHub Actions, or scripted into other automations without opening the full IDE. It supports the same range of underlying models as Cursor's desktop app, includes a shell mode for running commands with safety checks, and is meant for tasks like auto-updating docs, triggering security reviews, or building custom agents into CI pipelines.
cursor-cli.name: cursor-cli
cursor-cli.pricing_note: Shares Cursor's account and plan tiers (free Hobby tier, paid Pro/Pro+/Ultra/Teams plans)
requirements: A Cursor account
Network access to reach Cursor's model backend
A paid Cursor plan for extended agent usage
cursor-cli.tagline: Cursor's AI agents, running straight from your shell.
cursor-cli.youtube_title: The Cursor CLI is Actually Good!?

dbxcli-bin.description: dbxcli is Dropbox's own scriptable command-line client, built with the Go SDK, for listing, uploading, downloading, and otherwise managing files without leaving the terminal. It supports recursive transfers, piping data in and out, shared-link management, search, revisions, and JSON output for automation, plus team and member-scoped operations for business accounts. It's maintained by Dropbox engineers but explicitly noted as not an officially supported product.
dbxcli-bin.name: dbxcli-bin
requirements: A Dropbox account (OAuth login)
Network access
Dropbox storage limits and paid tiers still apply for how much you can store, separate from the tool itself
dbxcli-bin.tagline: Dropbox from the command line, scripts included.

dell-xps-touchpad-haptics.description: This package installs Omarchy's presets and control hooks for the Synaptics haptic touchpad found on newer Dell XPS laptops, exposing a Trigger > Hardware > Touchpad Haptics menu to switch the simulated click strength between low, mid, and high. It's a small, targeted driver-adjacent utility rather than a standalone app, only relevant if you're running Omarchy on the specific Dell XPS hardware it targets.
dell-xps-touchpad-haptics.name: dell-xps-touchpad-haptics
requirements: A Dell XPS laptop with a Synaptics haptic touchpad (only certain controller revisions, e.g. 06CB:D01A, are supported; newer 06CB:D01D units have reported compatibility issues)
Running the Omarchy desktop environment
dell-xps-touchpad-haptics.tagline: Dials in the click feel of Dell XPS haptic touchpads under Omarchy.

dropbox.description: Dropbox is a cloud storage and file-sharing service that syncs your files, photos, and documents across devices and lets you share or collaborate on them with others. It previews over 175 file types in the browser or app, supports large file transfers up to 250GB, and now layers in AI-assisted search and organization features alongside its core sync-and-share functionality.
dropbox.name: dropbox
dropbox.pricing_note: Basic tier is free with 2GB; Plus is $9.99/mo for 2TB; Standard $15/user/mo, Advanced $24/user/mo for teams, Enterprise is custom
requirements: A Dropbox account
Network access to sync files
dropbox.tagline: Cloud storage that follows your files everywhere.

dropbox-cli.description: dropbox-cli is a command-line control script for the official Dropbox desktop client on Linux, used to start, stop, or check the status of the Dropbox sync daemon, manage selective sync exclusions, and throttle bandwidth, all from a terminal without opening a GUI. It's a companion to the main Dropbox app rather than a replacement for it.
dropbox-cli.name: dropbox-cli
dropbox-cli.pricing_note: GPL-3.0-or-later licensed control script; it manages the Dropbox client, which itself has free and paid storage tiers
requirements: The Dropbox daemon/client installed and running
A Dropbox account
Network access
dropbox-cli.tagline: Terminal controls for the Dropbox desktop daemon.

elephant.description: Elephant is a headless data-provider and executor service that acts as a shared backend for building custom application launchers and desktop utilities on Linux. It aggregates data from a plugin-based set of providers (apps, files, clipboard, Bluetooth, calculator, package search, and more) and exposes them over Unix sockets using Protocol Buffers, so a separate frontend like Walker can query it and render results. On its own, without a frontend and provider plugins installed, it does nothing visible.
elephant.name: elephant
requirements: A frontend launcher (such as Walker) to actually see and use its results
Individual provider plugins for the data sources you want (apps, files, clipboard, etc.) — the base package alone has none installed
A systemd-based Linux environment is expected, though it can run standalone
elephant.tagline: The backend brain behind fast Linux application launchers.

elephant-all.description: elephant-all is a convenience package that installs the Elephant launcher backend together with its full set of official data providers in one shot, including desktop applications, files, clipboard history, Bluetooth, calculator, Arch package search, todo lists, bookmarks, Unicode symbols, window management, and web search. It exists because installing bare Elephant alone leaves a launcher frontend with nothing to search, since no providers ship by default.
elephant-all.name: elephant-all
requirements: A frontend launcher (such as Walker) to actually present and interact with results
A systemd-based Linux environment is expected, though it can run standalone
elephant-all.tagline: Elephant plus every official provider, bundled in one install.

elephant-archlinuxpkgs.description: Elephant is a backend daemon (used by launchers like Walker) that exposes different data sources as "providers" over a Unix socket. This package adds the Arch Linux package provider, letting the launcher search official repo and AUR packages and trigger install/remove actions without opening a terminal.
elephant-archlinuxpkgs.name: elephant-archlinuxpkgs
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker to actually use it
pacman/AUR helper on the system for package operations
elephant-archlinuxpkgs.tagline: Search and install Arch and AUR packages right from your launcher.

elephant-bluetooth.description: This is elephant's Bluetooth provider, giving any elephant-powered launcher a way to list, pair, connect, and disconnect Bluetooth devices as searchable/selectable items instead of switching to a separate settings app.
elephant-bluetooth.name: elephant-bluetooth
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
A Bluetooth adapter and a working BlueZ/system Bluetooth stack
elephant-bluetooth.tagline: Manage Bluetooth devices from the same launcher you open apps with.

elephant-calc.description: The calculator/unit-conversion provider for elephant. It lets a launcher evaluate arithmetic expressions and unit conversions as you type, so results appear live in the search results instead of needing a separate calculator app.
elephant-calc.name: elephant-calc
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
elephant-calc.tagline: Type a math expression, get the answer instantly.

elephant-clipboard.description: This provider gives elephant access to clipboard history, tracking previously copied text and images so a launcher frontend can search and re-paste earlier clipboard entries rather than only the most recent item.
elephant-clipboard.name: elephant-clipboard
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
A clipboard manager backend (e.g. wl-clipboard/cliphist on Wayland) actually recording history
elephant-clipboard.tagline: Search your clipboard history, including past images.

elephant-desktopapplications.description: This is elephant's core application-launching provider: it parses .desktop entries, tracks launch history/frequency, and exposes your installed applications so a launcher frontend like Walker can search for and open them. For most users this is the most essential of the elephant providers.
elephant-desktopapplications.name: elephant-desktopapplications
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
elephant-desktopapplications.tagline: The provider that turns your installed apps into launcher results.

elephant-files.description: The file-browsing provider for elephant. It lets a launcher frontend navigate directories, preview files, and perform basic file operations like opening or copying, turning the launcher into a lightweight file finder alongside its usual app-launching role.
elephant-files.name: elephant-files
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
elephant-files.tagline: Browse, preview, and open files without leaving your launcher.

elephant-menus.description: This provider lets you define custom, user-configured menus of actions or shortcuts that show up as selectable entries in an elephant-powered launcher, useful for scripts, quick toggles, or workflows you want one keystroke away.
elephant-menus.name: elephant-menus
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
User-authored menu configuration to be useful beyond defaults
elephant-menus.tagline: Build your own custom quick-action menus for the launcher.

elephant-providerlist.description: A meta-provider that lists elephant's available providers so a launcher frontend can offer a way to jump between them (e.g. switching from app search to file search) directly within the launcher's interface.
elephant-providerlist.name: elephant-providerlist
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
Other elephant providers installed to have anything to switch between
elephant-providerlist.tagline: Lets you switch between elephant's other providers on the fly.

elephant-runner.description: The command-runner provider for elephant: it scans your PATH and lets you type and execute arbitrary shell commands as launcher results, similar to a run dialog but integrated into the same search interface used for apps and files.
elephant-runner.name: elephant-runner
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
elephant-runner.tagline: Run shell commands straight from your launcher's search bar.

elephant-symbols.description: This provider supplies elephant's symbol and emoji picker data, covering multi-locale unicode names so you can search for a symbol or emoji by description and insert it. Its larger install size reflects the bundled unicode/locale symbol database compared to the other, mostly code-only providers.
elephant-symbols.name: elephant-symbols
requirements: A running elephant daemon and a frontend such as Walker
elephant-symbols.tagline: Find and insert emoji and unicode symbols by name, in any language.

elephant-todo.description: Elephant is a background data-provider service (communicating over Unix sockets and Protocol Buffers) that powers application launchers and desktop widgets on Linux. The todo provider is one of its plugins, letting a launcher frontend add items, mark them active or done, set due times, and surface notifications, all without its own window; you interact with it through whatever launcher UI is connected to Elephant.
elephant-todo.name: elephant-todo
requirements: The Elephant backend service running (elephant-unicode/websearch are separate provider plugins, not needed for this one)
A launcher frontend that talks to Elephant over its Unix socket to actually see or use the todo list
elephant-todo.tagline: Turns Elephant's launcher backend into a quick-capture task list.

elephant-unicode.description: This is a plugin for Elephant, a headless provider service that Linux application launchers query over Unix sockets. The unicode provider lets a connected launcher search and insert unicode symbols and emoji across multiple locales. It has no interface of its own; a launcher frontend (like a custom Omarchy menu) displays the results.
elephant-unicode.name: elephant-unicode
requirements: The Elephant backend service running
A launcher frontend connected to Elephant to actually browse or pick symbols
elephant-unicode.tagline: Emoji and unicode symbol lookup for the Elephant launcher backend.

elephant-websearch.description: This is a plugin for Elephant, a headless data-provider service Linux launchers query over Unix sockets. The websearch provider lets you define custom search engines and trigger web queries straight from a connected launcher, without opening a browser first. Like the rest of Elephant, it runs as a background service with no GUI of its own.
elephant-websearch.name: elephant-websearch
requirements: The Elephant backend service running
A launcher frontend connected to Elephant, and a browser to open the resulting search
elephant-websearch.tagline: Custom web search shortcuts for the Elephant launcher backend.

flea.description: Flea is a native file manager built specifically for the Omarchy Hyprland desktop, pairing a Rust backend with a Quickshell frontend rather than extending an existing manager like Nautilus. It supports vim-style keyboard navigation, list/columns/grid views, rich previews (images, video, PDFs, archives), undoable file operations, and network mounts (SMB/NFS, Taildrop, Dropbox), all styled to match Omarchy's live color palette.
flea.name: flea
requirements: Runs on Omarchy with Quickshell 0.3.1+
Optional tools for extra features: bubblewrap/util-linux for thumbnailing, bsdtar/7z for archives, gio for network mounts, Qt PDF/Multimedia modules for previews
flea.tagline: The fastest, keyboard-first file manager built for Omarchy.

github-copilot-cli.description: GitHub Copilot CLI brings GitHub's Copilot coding agent into the terminal, letting you describe what you want in natural language and have it read, edit, and run code in your project. It can pull in context from your GitHub repositories, issues, and pull requests, extends via MCP for custom tools, and previews every action for you to approve before it runs. It is entirely command-line, with no window of its own.
github-copilot-cli.name: github-copilot-cli
github-copilot-cli.pricing_note: requires an active GitHub Copilot subscription
requirements: A GitHub account
An active GitHub Copilot subscription
Network access to GitHub
github-copilot-cli.tagline: GitHub Copilot's coding agent, right in your terminal.
github-copilot-cli.youtube_title: The ultimate guide to the GitHub Copilot CLI | Full demo | GitHub Checkout

gpu-screen-recorder.description: gpu-screen-recorder is a lightweight, high-performance screen recorder for Linux that offloads capture and encoding to the GPU, minimizing the performance hit compared to typical CPU-based recorders. It works on both X11 and Wayland across AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA GPUs (plus Apple Silicon via Asahi Linux with software encoding), and supports plain recording, live streaming, instant-replay clips, and screenshots. This package is the core command-line tool; a separate GTK-based GUI exists as its own project.
gpu-screen-recorder.name: gpu-screen-recorder
requirements: A supported GPU driver (AMD, Intel, or NVIDIA) for hardware-accelerated encoding
gpu-screen-recorder.tagline: Shadowplay-style, GPU-accelerated screen recording for Linux.

grok-bot.description: Grok Bot is xAI's always-on AI agent product: each Bot you create gets a persistent cloud virtual machine with its own browser, filesystem, and terminal, and can sign into your tools and apps to carry out multi-step work, resuming after you close your device. You can watch a live screen-share of what a Bot is doing, and access the same Bot from desktop or mobile. It uses a permission-escalation model, starting read-only and gaining write/execute access as it proves reliable.
grok-bot.name: grok-bot
grok-bot.pricing_note: bundled into paid tiers such as SuperGrok Heavy ($300/mo), Cursor Ultra ($200/mo), or Cursor Teams Premium ($120/seat/mo); no free tier at launch
requirements: An xAI/X account
One of the qualifying paid subscription tiers
Network access for the persistent cloud VM
grok-bot.tagline: An always-on AI teammate with its own persistent cloud computer.

herdr.description: Herdr is a Rust-based terminal session manager purpose-built for running multiple AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and similar tools) at once. It works like tmux or screen, keeping sessions alive through disconnects or reboots and letting you reattach from anywhere, but it also detects each agent's state, working, blocked, done, or idle, and shows it in a sidebar so you're not hunting for a stuck agent. It runs inside your existing terminal (ghostty, alacritty, kitty, wezterm) with no Electron overhead.
herdr.name: herdr
herdr.tagline: One terminal that keeps every AI coding agent running and visible.

hermes-desktop.description: Hermes Agent is an open-source AI agent from Nous Research that is built around a learning loop: it creates and improves its own skills from experience, persists knowledge across sessions, and searches its own past conversations. Hermes Desktop is the native app version of it for macOS, Windows, and Linux, giving you a local window onto the same agent that's also reachable through Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and email. It can run against Nous Portal, OpenRouter, OpenAI, or your own model endpoint.
hermes-desktop.name: hermes-desktop
hermes-desktop.pricing_note: the app itself is free and open-source (MIT), but it needs an LLM provider; either your own API keys or a paid Nous Portal subscription that bundles model and tool access
requirements: An API key for an LLM provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, etc.) or a Nous Portal subscription
Network access
hermes-desktop.tagline: A native desktop shell for Nous Research's self-improving Hermes agent.

heroic-games-launcher-bin.description: Heroic Games Launcher is a free, open-source alternative launcher for Linux, Windows, and macOS (plus Steam Deck) that brings your Epic Games, GOG, and Amazon Prime Gaming libraries together in one app. It handles downloads and install queues with live progress, lets you manage Wine/Proton compatibility tools for running Windows games, offers a controller-friendly full-screen console mode for TVs and handhelds, and supports custom cover art and multiple language and theme options.
heroic-games-launcher-bin.name: heroic-games-launcher-bin
requirements: Accounts on whichever storefronts you want to use: Epic Games, GOG, and/or Amazon Prime Gaming
Network access to those storefronts
heroic-games-launcher-bin.tagline: One free launcher for your Epic, GOG, and Amazon Prime game libraries.
heroic-games-launcher-bin.youtube_title: Heroic Games Launcher on Linux Demo

hey-cli.description: HEY CLI is Basecamp's official command-line and text-based interface for the HEY email service. It gives terminal users a full-screen TUI (run with `hey tui`) for Mail, Contacts, Calendar, and Journal, using HEY's own keyboard shortcuts, alongside individual CLI commands for scripting things like composing, searching, and watching for new mail as JSON. It also ships as a skill and MCP server so AI coding agents like Claude can read and act on your HEY mail directly.
hey-cli.name: hey-cli
hey-cli.pricing_note: the CLI itself is free and open source (MIT); it requires a paid HEY.com email subscription to be useful
requirements: an active HEY.com email account/subscription
browser-based sign-in to authenticate the CLI
network access to sync with HEY
hey-cli.tagline: Your HEY inbox, calendar, and contacts, without leaving the terminal.

hyprland-preview-share-picker.description: This is a drop-in replacement for Hyprland's default screen-share picker. Instead of a bare text list, it shows live thumbnail previews of every open window and every connected monitor in a tabbed GTK4 window, so you can visually confirm what you're about to share over video calls or screen recordings. It plugs into the standard XDG desktop portal for Hyprland and its look can be themed with a custom stylesheet.
hyprland-preview-share-picker.name: hyprland-preview-share-picker
requirements: Hyprland window manager
xdg-desktop-portal-hyprland
GTK4 and GTK4 Layer Shell installed
slurp (optional, for manual region selection)
hyprland-preview-share-picker.tagline: Pick exactly the window or monitor you're sharing, by actually seeing it first.

hyprland-preview-share-picker-git.description: This is the git/development-snapshot build of hyprland-preview-share-picker, Hyprland's alternative screen-share picker. It replaces the default text-only picker with live thumbnail previews of open windows and connected monitors in a tabbed GTK4 window, so you can confirm what you're sharing before a call or recording starts. Being the -git package, it tracks the latest unreleased commits rather than a tagged release.
hyprland-preview-share-picker-git.name: hyprland-preview-share-picker-git
requirements: Hyprland window manager
xdg-desktop-portal-hyprland
GTK4 and GTK4 Layer Shell installed
slurp (optional, for manual region selection)
Rust nightly toolchain to build from source
hyprland-preview-share-picker-git.tagline: Pick exactly the window or monitor you're sharing, by actually seeing it first.

hyprshade.description: Hyprshade is a command-line tool that manages Hyprland's built-in screen-shader feature, letting you turn visual filters like a blue-light-reduction warm filter on or off, or switch between them automatically based on time of day. It's meant as a Wayland-native replacement for older tools like Redshift or f.lux, and comes with a default blue-light shader plus support for custom GLSL shaders and systemd-based scheduling.
hyprshade.name: hyprshade
requirements: Hyprland window manager with screen_shader support
systemd (only if using the scheduling/auto feature)
hyprshade.tagline: Automatic blue-light filtering and screen shaders for Hyprland, on a schedule.

intel-ipu7-camera.description: This package builds and installs the driver stack needed to make the OV08X40 MIPI camera work on specific Intel 'Hurrican/Performance' reference laptops, using Intel's IPU7 hardware image signal processor (ISP). It's a hardware-enablement/installer package: it compiles kernel patches and firmware integration rather than providing any user-facing app, and is only relevant if you own that specific hardware.
intel-ipu7-camera.name: intel-ipu7-camera
requirements: a Hurrican/Performance reference laptop with the OV08X40 camera and Intel IPU7 ISP
root privileges to build kernel modules and install firmware
a compatible kernel (project targets kernel 6.19.6-series patches)
intel-ipu7-camera.tagline: Gets the built-in webcam working on Intel Hurrican/Performance laptops.

intel-lpmd.description: Intel's Low Power Mode Daemon watches how busy your system is and, on light workloads like idling or basic browsing, steers work onto a more power-efficient subset of CPU cores to cut idle power draw, then restores full CPU capacity when demand rises. It runs quietly in the background as a systemd service and is configured and monitored through a companion command-line control tool or D-Bus, with no graphical interface.
intel-lpmd.name: intel-lpmd
requirements: a supported Intel CPU/platform
must be explicitly enabled via config or the intel_lpmd_control tool (disabled by default)
intel-lpmd.tagline: Squeezes extra battery life out of Intel laptops during light workloads.

lib32-nvidia-580xx-utils.description: This package provides the 32-bit companion utilities and shared libraries for NVIDIA's proprietary 580xx driver branch, needed so that 32-bit applications and games (commonly run through Steam/Proton on a 64-bit system) can talk to an NVIDIA GPU correctly. It has no interface of its own; it just supplies libraries other 32-bit programs link against. The 580 driver branch is NVIDIA's current long-lived branch, notable for improved Wayland support and being the last branch to support older Maxwell/Pascal/Volta GPUs.
lib32-nvidia-580xx-utils.name: lib32-nvidia-580xx-utils
lib32-nvidia-580xx-utils.pricing_note: proprietary driver, free to download and use, not open source
requirements: a supported NVIDIA GPU (matching the 580xx branch's supported architectures)
the matching 64-bit nvidia-580xx driver package installed alongside it
multilib/32-bit support enabled on the system
lib32-nvidia-580xx-utils.tagline: 32-bit helper tools and libraries for NVIDIA's 580-series Linux driver.

lib32-opencl-nvidia-580xx.description: This package installs NVIDIA's 32-bit OpenCL implementation for the 580xx proprietary driver branch, allowing 32-bit applications to run GPU-accelerated compute (OpenCL) workloads on an NVIDIA card. Like other lib32 packages it is purely a runtime library with no interface of its own, used by other software rather than run directly by a user.
lib32-opencl-nvidia-580xx.name: lib32-opencl-nvidia-580xx
lib32-opencl-nvidia-580xx.pricing_note: proprietary driver component, free to download and use, not open source
requirements: a supported NVIDIA GPU (matching the 580xx branch's supported architectures)
the matching nvidia-580xx driver installed
an OpenCL-using 32-bit application to actually invoke it
lib32-opencl-nvidia-580xx.tagline: 32-bit OpenCL support for NVIDIA GPUs on the 580-series driver.

libfprint-git.description: libfprint is the core software library that handles low-level communication with fingerprint scanning hardware and processes the fingerprint image data it captures. It is not something end users interact with directly; instead, system services like fprintd (which exposes fingerprint scanning over D-Bus) and desktop settings panels such as GNOME's Users settings build fingerprint login on top of it. This -git build tracks the current development branch with FocalTech MOC (Match-on-Chip) sensor support included, ahead of the stable release.
libfprint-git.name: libfprint-git
requirements: a supported fingerprint reader (e.g. FocalTech Match-on-Chip devices for this build)
a service like fprintd, plus desktop or PAM integration, to actually use it for login
libfprint-git.tagline: The library that lets Linux talk to your fingerprint reader.

libretro-cap32-git.description: This is Caprice32 packaged as a libretro core, letting RetroArch emulate the 1980s Amstrad CPC line of home computers, including the CPC 464, 464+, 6128, 6128+ and the GX4000 console variant. It plays original tape (CDT) and disk (DSK) images with autostart support, supports period keyboard layouts and joystick/lightgun input, and can use RetroArch's shaders for CRT-style visual effects. On its own it has no interface; it's a plugin loaded by RetroArch, which provides the actual on-screen menus.
libretro-cap32-git.name: libretro-cap32-git
requirements: RetroArch (or another libretro frontend) to actually run it
your own legally-owned Amstrad CPC game/software images, since none are bundled
libretro-cap32-git.tagline: Brings the classic Amstrad CPC home computer into RetroArch.

libretro-database-git.description: A collection of game databases and cheat-code files used by RetroArch and its emulator cores. It lets RetroArch verify that a ROM file is the genuine, correct version, assign it a clean display name, pull box-art thumbnails, and show metadata like developer, release year, and genre. The data is compiled from trusted preservation groups such as No-Intro, Redump, TOSEC, GameTDB, and MAME.
libretro-database-git.name: libretro-database-git
requirements: Used alongside RetroArch and its emulator cores; on its own it is just reference data with no interface
libretro-database-git.tagline: The shared catalog that lets RetroArch actually recognize your games.

libretro-fbneo-git.description: FinalBurn Neo (FBNeo) is a multi-system arcade emulator core packaged for RetroArch, continuing the earlier FinalBurn line of emulators. It accurately emulates classic arcade hardware including Capcom's CPS systems and Neo Geo, plus a handful of consoles, with support for netplay, rewind, and shader effects. As a libretro core it has no interface of its own — RetroArch loads it to run arcade ROMs you supply.
libretro-fbneo-git.name: libretro-fbneo-git
libretro-fbneo-git.pricing_note: custom license (see the project's license.txt), not a standard OSI license
requirements: Arcade ROM files matching the exact revisions FBNeo expects (not included and not distributed by the project)
RetroArch installed to load the core
libretro-fbneo-git.tagline: Bringing the arcade to your living room, one CPS and Neo Geo board at a time.

libretro-uae-git.description: PUAE-libretro is a work-in-progress port of the Amiga emulator UAE (based on WinUAE 5.3.1) to the libretro API, so RetroArch can boot and run classic Amiga software. It reads standard Amiga disk formats (ADF, ADZ, IPF, DMS, FDI), hard drive images, and CDs, with support for WHDLoad game packages, multi-disk M3U playlists, and remappable virtual-keyboard controls. It is a backend emulation core with no interface of its own.
libretro-uae-git.name: libretro-uae-git
requirements: Kickstart ROM files matching specific MD5 checksums for the Amiga model being emulated (A500, A1200, A4000, CD32, etc.) — not included
RetroArch installed to load the core
External CAPSIMG library for IPF copy-protected disk support
libretro-uae-git.tagline: A whole Commodore Amiga, folded into a single RetroArch core.

libretro-vice-x128-git.description: This package builds the Commodore 128 variant of the VICE (Versatile Commodore Emulator) core for RetroArch, letting it boot C128 software. VICE-libretro supports save states, ZIP archive loading, M3U multi-disk playlists, and optional JiffyDOS fast-loading ROMs. It is purely an emulation backend — you interact with it through RetroArch's own interface, not a UI of its own.
libretro-vice-x128-git.name: libretro-vice-x128-git
requirements: Commodore 128 software/disk images to run (not included)
RetroArch installed to load the core
Optional JiffyDOS ROM files for faster disk access

libretro-vice-x64-git.description: This is the 'fast' Commodore 64 core from VICE-libretro, a RetroArch port of the VICE emulator, tuned for speed over full cycle accuracy. It plays standard C64 disk and tape images, supports ZIP archives and M3U multi-disk playlists, and offers save states and remappable controls. Like all VICE cores it's a pure emulation backend with no interface of its own — RetroArch provides the front end.
libretro-vice-x64-git.name: libretro-vice-x64-git
requirements: Commodore 64 software/disk images to run (not included)
RetroArch installed to load the core
Optional JiffyDOS ROM files for faster disk access
libretro-vice-x64-git.tagline: The classic C64, running fast inside RetroArch.

libretro-vice-x64dtv-git.description: This VICE-libretro core emulates the Commodore 64 Direct-to-TV (C64DTV), the single-chip, joystick-shaped mini-console Commodore released with games built in. It's part of the same RetroArch port of VICE as the other Commodore cores, offering save states, ZIP/M3U support, and remappable controls. It has no interface of its own — RetroArch is the front end.
libretro-vice-x64dtv-git.name: libretro-vice-x64dtv-git
requirements: C64DTV-compatible software/images to run (not included)
RetroArch installed to load the core
libretro-vice-x64dtv-git.tagline: The plug-and-play Commodore 64 console, emulated in RetroArch.

libretro-vice-x64sc-git.description: This is the cycle-accurate 'sc' Commodore 64 core from VICE-libretro, prioritizing faithful timing and compatibility over raw speed. Built on the same RetroArch port of VICE as the other cores, it plays standard C64 disk and tape images with save states, ZIP archive support, and multi-disk M3U playlists. It's an emulation backend with no interface of its own — you run it through RetroArch.
libretro-vice-x64sc-git.name: libretro-vice-x64sc-git
requirements: Commodore 64 software/disk images to run (not included)
RetroArch installed to load the core
Optional JiffyDOS ROM files for faster disk access
libretro-vice-x64sc-git.tagline: The Commodore 64, emulated cycle-for-cycle inside RetroArch.

libretro-vice-xcbm2-git.description: This VICE-libretro core emulates the Commodore CBM-II 6x0/7x0 series, the business and professional-oriented 8-bit computers Commodore sold alongside the C64. It's part of the same RetroArch port of VICE as the other Commodore cores, with save states, disk/tape image support, and remappable controls, and has no interface of its own beyond RetroArch's.
libretro-vice-xcbm2-git.name: libretro-vice-xcbm2-git
requirements: CBM-II software/disk images to run (not included)
RetroArch installed to load the core
libretro-vice-xcbm2-git.tagline: Commodore's business-class 8-bit machine, alive again in RetroArch.

libretro-vice-xcbm5x0-git.description: This VICE-libretro core emulates the Commodore CBM-II 5x0 series, a lower-end, home-computer-styled variant of Commodore's professional CBM-II line. Built on the same RetroArch port of VICE as the other cores, it supports save states, disk/tape image loading, and remappable controls, with no interface beyond what RetroArch provides.
libretro-vice-xcbm5x0-git.name: libretro-vice-xcbm5x0-git
requirements: CBM-II 5x0 software/disk images to run (not included)
RetroArch installed to load the core
libretro-vice-xcbm5x0-git.tagline: The compact CBM-II, emulated inside RetroArch.

libretro-vice-xpet-git.description: This VICE-libretro core emulates the Commodore PET, one of the earliest personal computers Commodore released in the late 1970s. It's part of the same RetroArch port of VICE as the other Commodore cores, offering save states, disk/tape image support, and configurable controls, with no interface of its own — it runs entirely inside RetroArch.
libretro-vice-xpet-git.name: libretro-vice-xpet-git
requirements: Commodore PET software/disk images to run (not included)
RetroArch installed to load the core
libretro-vice-xpet-git.tagline: One of Commodore's very first computers, running again in RetroArch.

libretro-vice-xplus4-git.description: This is the Plus/4 core of VICE (the Versatile Commodore Emulator) built for the libretro/RetroArch framework. It lets RetroArch load and run Commodore Plus/4 software, cycle-accurate down to the original hardware, so old Plus/4 disk and tape images can be played on a modern Linux desktop. It has no interface of its own; it plugs into RetroArch, which supplies the menus, controller mapping, and video output.
libretro-vice-xplus4-git.name: libretro-vice-xplus4-git
requirements: RetroArch installed to load and run the core
Plus/4 software/ROM images supplied by the user
libretro-vice-xplus4-git.tagline: Bring the Commodore Plus/4 back to life inside RetroArch.

libretro-vice-xscpu64-git.description: This is the SuperCPU core of VICE (the Versatile Commodore Emulator) built for the libretro/RetroArch framework. It emulates a Commodore 64 fitted with the SuperCPU accelerator cartridge, which boosted the C64's clock speed far beyond the stock 1MHz. It is a RetroArch plug-in core with no interface of its own; RetroArch handles loading software and displaying it.
libretro-vice-xscpu64-git.name: libretro-vice-xscpu64-git
requirements: RetroArch installed to load and run the core
C64/SuperCPU software or ROM images supplied by the user
libretro-vice-xscpu64-git.tagline: Emulate the souped-up Commodore 64 SuperCPU inside RetroArch.

libretro-vice-xvic-git.description: This is the VIC-20 core of VICE (the Versatile Commodore Emulator) built for the libretro/RetroArch framework. It emulates Commodore's 1980-era VIC-20 home computer so its games and programs can run inside RetroArch on a modern Linux machine. As a libretro core it has no standalone window or menu of its own; RetroArch provides the surrounding interface.
libretro-vice-xvic-git.name: libretro-vice-xvic-git
requirements: RetroArch installed to load and run the core
VIC-20 software/ROM images supplied by the user
libretro-vice-xvic-git.tagline: Play Commodore VIC-20 software straight from RetroArch.

limine-mkinitcpio-hook.description: This package hooks limine-entry-tool into mkinitcpio so that installing, updating, or removing a kernel automatically regenerates the corresponding Limine bootloader entry, including unified kernel images and fallback images. It writes and prunes entries by machine-id and periodically backs up limine.conf, removing the need to hand-edit boot configuration after a kernel update.
limine-mkinitcpio-hook.name: limine-mkinitcpio-hook
requirements: Limine bootloader version 8 or newer
A FAT32 EFI/boot partition with at least 1 GiB free
mkinitcpio-based kernel install workflow
efibootmgr for UEFI systems
limine-mkinitcpio-hook.tagline: Keeps Limine's boot menu in sync every time you install a kernel.

limine-snapper-sync.description: This tool bridges the Snapper snapshot manager and the Limine bootloader on Btrfs systems: whenever a Snapper snapshot is created or deleted, it automatically adds or removes a matching bootable entry in Limine, complete with the right kernel files. It can also restore the system from a chosen snapshot (via rsync, file replace, or Snapper) and creates a safety backup entry after a restore so you can undo it, plus it checks bootable files for corruption.
limine-snapper-sync.name: limine-snapper-sync
requirements: Limine bootloader version 8 or newer
Snapper and btrfs-progs installed on a Btrfs root
A FAT32 boot partition, 4 GB or more recommended
limine-snapper-sync.tagline: Turns every Btrfs snapshot into a bootable Limine menu entry.

link-studio.description: Link Studio is an open-source, unofficial Linux app for controlling Insta360 Link webcams, filling the gap left by Insta360's Windows/macOS-only software. It gives direct access to the camera's pan, tilt, zoom, autofocus, and privacy-mode controls, plus its built-in AI tracking modes (like Whiteboard and DeskView), alongside live preview, H.264 recording, and local effects such as background blur and green screen. It's built with GTK4 and libadwaita, so it follows your desktop's light/dark theme, and it can also act as a virtual camera and offer optional offline transcription of voice notes.
link-studio.name: link-studio
requirements: An Insta360 Link or Link 2 webcam (hardware-tested with Link 2)
GTK4, libadwaita, V4L2/UVC, GStreamer, PipeWire, OpenCV and MediaPipe on the system
link-studio.tagline: A native Linux control panel for your Insta360 Link webcam.

linux-mainline-panther-lake.description: This package builds the Linux mainline kernel (the newest, still-in-development upstream branch tracked at kernel.org) with the audio driver work needed for Intel's Panther Lake laptop chips. It exists for people who want the very latest kernel changes rather than a stable release, on hardware new enough that its audio hasn't yet landed in a standard Arch kernel build.
linux-mainline-panther-lake.name: linux-mainline-panther-lake
requirements: An Intel Panther Lake-based laptop to benefit from the audio support
Comfort running an unstable/mainline kernel and its module headers
linux-mainline-panther-lake.tagline: The bleeding-edge upstream kernel, built with Panther Lake audio support baked in.

linux-mainline-panther-lake-headers.description: This package supplies the kernel headers and build scripts needed to compile external kernel modules (like proprietary drivers or DKMS packages) against the linux-mainline-panther-lake kernel. It has no functionality on its own; it exists purely to support building modules for that specific kernel build.
linux-mainline-panther-lake-headers.name: linux-mainline-panther-lake-headers
requirements: The matching linux-mainline-panther-lake kernel installed
Only needed if compiling third-party kernel modules
linux-mainline-panther-lake-headers.tagline: The build headers that pair with the Panther Lake mainline kernel.

linux-ptl.description: linux-ptl is a specially patched Linux kernel built for Intel Panther Lake laptops (such as the Dell XPS Panther Lake line) that packages roughly twenty hardware backports ahead of their arrival in a standard stable kernel. It focuses on fixes for Panel Replay power management and OLED variable refresh rate (VRR), the kind of day-one enablement work that lets brand-new silicon run properly on Linux before upstream stable catches up. It was built through collaboration between Intel, Dell, and the Omarchy project and is meant to be a stopgap until mainline Linux fully absorbs the changes.
linux-ptl.name: linux-ptl
requirements: An Intel Panther Lake-based laptop (e.g. Dell XPS Panther Lake) to see any benefit
linux-ptl.tagline: A custom Arch kernel giving new Intel Panther Lake laptops day-one Linux support.

linux-ptl-audio.description: linux-ptl-audio is a variant of the Panther Lake enablement kernel that backports SDCA (SoundWire Device Class for Audio) driver support so speakers and microphones work correctly on new Intel Panther Lake laptops. Like its sibling linux-ptl, it exists to give very new hardware working audio on Linux before those fixes land in a standard stable kernel release.
linux-ptl-audio.name: linux-ptl-audio
requirements: An Intel Panther Lake-based laptop with SoundWire/SDCA audio hardware to see any benefit
linux-ptl-audio.tagline: The Panther Lake kernel variant focused purely on getting sound working.

linux-ptl-audio-headers.description: This package ships the kernel headers and build scripts that pair with a specific Arch Linux kernel build carrying SDCA audio backports for Intel Panther Lake laptops. It contains no runtime software of its own; DKMS and other tools use it to compile kernel modules (like proprietary drivers) against that exact kernel version. It only matters if you are running that particular kernel and need to build a module for it.
linux-ptl-audio-headers.name: linux-ptl-audio-headers
requirements: Only useful when running the matching linux-ptl-audio kernel package
Intel Panther Lake hardware for the audio fixes to be relevant
linux-ptl-audio-headers.tagline: The build-time headers for Arch's Panther Lake audio kernel, needed to compile out-of-tree kernel modules.

linux-ptl-headers.description: Like other kernel-headers packages, this provides the compiled headers and scripts needed to build kernel modules against a specific custom Arch kernel, in this case one patched for Intel Panther Lake laptops with Panel Replay power-saving and OLED variable refresh rate fixes. There is nothing to launch or configure directly; it exists purely to support DKMS module builds for that kernel.
linux-ptl-headers.name: linux-ptl-headers
requirements: Only useful when running the matching linux-ptl kernel package
Intel Panther Lake hardware with an OLED / Panel Replay-capable display for the fixes to apply
linux-ptl-headers.tagline: Build headers for Arch's Panther Lake kernel variant with Panel Replay and OLED VRR display fixes.

lmstudio.description: LM Studio is a desktop app for browsing, downloading, and running large language models locally, so your prompts and data never leave your computer. It offers a ChatGPT-style chat interface with threads and folders, an OpenAI-compatible local API server for developers, and a model browser that pulls open models from Hugging Face. It can also connect out to larger cloud models when you want them, but local, offline inference is the core pitch.
lmstudio.name: lmstudio
lmstudio.pricing_note: free for personal and commercial use, no premium tiers
requirements: Enough disk space and RAM/VRAM to hold whichever local model you download
A capable GPU (or Apple Silicon) speeds up inference but is not strictly required
Network access only when browsing or downloading models from Hugging Face; runs fully offline afterward
lmstudio.tagline: Discover, download, and chat with open-source AI models entirely on your own machine.
lmstudio.youtube_title: Getting started with LM Studio (100% private local AI)

lmstudio-bin.description: This is the same LM Studio desktop app as the source-build package, just distributed as a ready-to-run binary instead of being compiled from source at install time. It lets you discover, download, and chat with open-source language models locally through a ChatGPT-style interface, keeping all inference on your own hardware.
lmstudio-bin.name: lmstudio-bin
lmstudio-bin.pricing_note: free for personal and commercial use, no premium tiers
requirements: Enough disk space and RAM/VRAM to hold whichever local model you download
A capable GPU (or Apple Silicon) speeds up inference but is not strictly required
Network access only when browsing or downloading models from Hugging Face; runs fully offline afterward
lmstudio-bin.tagline: The prebuilt-binary package of LM Studio, for running local AI models without waiting on a build.
lmstudio-bin.youtube_title: Getting started with LM Studio (100% private local AI)

localsend.description: LocalSend lets you send files and messages between nearby devices - phones, laptops, desktops, whatever - over your local Wi-Fi, without needing the internet or any cloud account. It uses an encrypted REST API over HTTPS to move files directly between devices, and works across Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS. Think of it as a free, cross-platform, privacy-respecting AirDrop.
localsend.name: localsend
requirements: Sending device must be reachable over a local network (Wi-Fi/LAN) with the receiving device
localsend.tagline: An open-source AirDrop alternative that beams files across any platform over your local network.

localsend-bin.description: Same app as the localsend source package: a free, open-source, cross-platform tool for beaming files and messages between nearby devices over a local network, with no cloud account or internet connection required. This variant is packaged as a precompiled binary for a faster install.
localsend-bin.name: localsend-bin
requirements: Sending device must be reachable over a local network (Wi-Fi/LAN) with the receiving device
localsend-bin.tagline: The prebuilt-binary package of LocalSend, ready to send files across your network without a build step.

macbook12-spi-driver-dkms.description: This DKMS package builds and installs the input driver for the SPI-connected keyboard and touchpad found in the 12-inch MacBook (2015+) and the 2016-2018 MacBook Pro (13-inch and 15-inch Touch Bar models). Basic keyboard and trackpad support has since been merged into the mainline Linux kernel, so today this package is mainly useful for its extras: Touch Bar support (with idle dimming), the ambient light sensor, and low-level packet tracing for debugging.
macbook12-spi-driver-dkms.name: macbook12-spi-driver-dkms
requirements: A 12-inch MacBook (2015 or later) or a 2016-2018 MacBook Pro (13"/15") to have any effect
DKMS set up so the module rebuilds automatically on kernel updates
macbook12-spi-driver-dkms.tagline: Kernel driver that brings the keyboard, trackpad, Touch Bar, and light sensor of newer MacBooks to Linux.

macbook8-spi-pxa2xx-nodma-dkms.description: This is a modified version of the Intel PXA2xx SPI PCI driver, patched specifically to force PIO (programmed I/O) mode for the Wildcat Point GSPI controller (PCI ID 8086:9ce6) found in the MacBook8,1 (early 2015 12-inch MacBook). It exists as a workaround for DMA-related issues on that exact chipset so the SPI-attached keyboard and trackpad function correctly. It is distributed through the Omarchy project's package repository rather than upstream, and has no interface of its own - it is a background kernel module.
macbook8-spi-pxa2xx-nodma-dkms.name: macbook8-spi-pxa2xx-nodma-dkms
requirements: A MacBook8,1 (2015 12-inch MacBook) with the Wildcat Point GSPI controller (8086:9ce6)
DKMS to rebuild the module across kernel updates
macbook8-spi-pxa2xx-nodma-dkms.tagline: A patched SPI driver that forces PIO mode so the 2015 MacBook's touchpad and keyboard work reliably on Linux.

makima-bin.description: Makima is a Linux daemon that intercepts input from keyboards, mice, game controllers, and tablets (via the evdev kernel interface) and remaps them - individual keys, button combos, analog sticks - into other keys, key sequences, or shell commands. It can even auto-switch remapping profiles based on which window is focused, on Hyprland, Sway, Niri, or X11. There is no graphical interface; everything is configured by hand-editing TOML files under ~/.config/makima/ and restarting the service.
makima-bin.name: makima-bin
requirements: The uinput kernel module, for creating virtual input devices
Systemd, if installed as a service (manual execution is also possible)
kdotool, optionally, for per-window layout switching on Plasma Wayland
makima-bin.tagline: A background daemon that remaps keys, buttons, and macros for any keyboard, mouse, or controller on Linux.

minecraft-launcher.description: The official Minecraft Launcher is the app Mojang provides for installing, updating, and launching Minecraft: Java Edition (and linking to Bedrock Edition) on your computer. You sign in with a Microsoft account, choose a game version and modpack profile, and the launcher handles downloading and keeping the game up to date. The launcher itself is free to use, but playing the full game requires either owning Minecraft or an active Xbox Game Pass subscription; a short free trial (about 100 minutes) is available without a purchase.
minecraft-launcher.name: minecraft-launcher
minecraft-launcher.pricing_note: launcher is free; playing requires buying Minecraft (one-time) or an Xbox Game Pass subscription, after a ~100-minute free trial
requirements: A free Microsoft account to sign in
A Minecraft purchase or Xbox Game Pass subscription to play beyond the free trial
Network access to download the game and verify your account
minecraft-launcher.tagline: Mojang's official launcher for downloading, updating, and starting Minecraft with your Microsoft account.

mise-bin.description: mise is a command-line tool that replaces a pile of separate version managers (like nvm, pyenv, rbenv) with one binary. It installs and switches between versions of programming languages and dev tools per project, loads project-specific environment variables automatically when you cd into a directory, and can define and run project tasks, all driven by a single mise.toml config file.
mise-bin.name: mise-bin
mise-bin.tagline: One CLI to install your dev tools, load your env vars, and run your project tasks.

nautilus-dropbox.description: This package integrates the Dropbox desktop client with the GNOME Files (Nautilus) file manager, adding sync-status overlay icons and right-click context menu options (like Share Dropbox Link) directly in your normal file browsing. It requires the separate Dropbox daemon to actually be installed and running, and a Dropbox account to sign in and sync files.
nautilus-dropbox.name: nautilus-dropbox
requirements: A Dropbox account (sign up/log in)
The Dropbox sync daemon installed and running
Network access to sync files
nautilus-dropbox.tagline: Brings Dropbox's sync status and sharing menu right into your file manager.

nautilus-open-any-terminal.description: A small Nautilus (and Caja) extension that adds an "Open Terminal Here" context-menu entry, but lets you choose which of 40+ terminal emulators it launches, such as Kitty, Alacritty, Konsole, or Tilix, instead of being stuck with GNOME Terminal. It also supports custom launch commands for more specialized setups.
nautilus-open-any-terminal.name: nautilus-open-any-terminal
requirements: Nautilus or Caja file manager
nautilus-python (or python3-nautilus) support
A terminal emulator to launch
nautilus-open-any-terminal.tagline: Right-click any folder and pop open the terminal you actually use.

nordvpn-bin.description: This is NordVPN's official command-line client for Linux, letting you connect to NordVPN's VPN servers, enable a kill switch, set up split tunneling, and manage settings without a graphical app. The CLI itself is free to install, but connecting to actual VPN servers requires logging into a paid NordVPN account, the app's free Meshnet feature is the exception.
nordvpn-bin.name: nordvpn-bin
nordvpn-bin.pricing_note: app is free to install; VPN server access needs a paid NordVPN plan (from about $3.49/mo on longer terms)
requirements: A NordVPN account
An active paid NordVPN subscription to use the VPN servers
Network access
nordvpn-bin.tagline: Encrypt and route your traffic through NordVPN's global network, right from the terminal.

nvidia-580xx-dkms.description: This package provides the NVIDIA 580xx-series proprietary kernel module source, built automatically against your running kernel via DKMS. It's the low-level piece that lets the Linux kernel drive an NVIDIA graphics card; the 580 branch is a current driver series used for recent GPU generations. It has no interface of its own, it just needs to be present for the matching nvidia-580xx-utils package (and your GPU) to work.
nvidia-580xx-dkms.name: nvidia-580xx-dkms
nvidia-580xx-dkms.pricing_note: driver is free to use, distributed under NVIDIA's custom license, not open source
requirements: An NVIDIA GPU compatible with the 580xx driver branch
A Linux kernel with DKMS support
Matching nvidia-580xx-utils package
nvidia-580xx-dkms.tagline: Kernel module sources so your Linux kernel can talk to your NVIDIA GPU.

nvidia-580xx-utils.description: This package supplies the user-space side of NVIDIA's proprietary 580xx driver: the OpenGL/Vulkan/CUDA libraries, nvidia-smi, and Xorg driver bits that applications and games rely on to talk to an NVIDIA GPU. It pairs with nvidia-580xx-dkms (the kernel module) to form a complete driver stack for a compatible NVIDIA card.
nvidia-580xx-utils.name: nvidia-580xx-utils
nvidia-580xx-utils.pricing_note: driver is free to use, distributed under NVIDIA's custom license, not open source
requirements: An NVIDIA GPU compatible with the 580xx driver branch
Matching nvidia-580xx-dkms kernel module package
nvidia-580xx-utils.tagline: The user-space libraries and tools that make the NVIDIA 580xx driver actually usable.

omacalc.description: Omacalc is a minimal calculator app built with Qt Quick and C++, made for the Omarchy desktop. It handles standard arithmetic with proper operator precedence, decimals, percentages, and sign toggling, showing your typed expression above the result so you can double-check your input. It automatically follows your system's Omarchy theme and light/dark mode, and supports full keyboard entry.
omacalc.name: omacalc
requirements: xdg-desktop-portal with a backend
omacalc.tagline: A calculator that gets out of your way and matches your desktop theme.

omacut.description: Omacut is a bare-bones video trimmer built with Qt Quick and ffmpeg. You open a video, drag start and end handles to select the section you want, preview it, and export as MP4 at its original resolution, 1080p, or 720p, always keeping the original aspect ratio. It's built for quick trims rather than full editing, with keyboard shortcuts for playback, frame-stepping, and zooming.
omacut.name: omacut
requirements: ffmpeg and ffprobe installed on PATH
xdg-desktop-portal with a backend for file selection
omacut.tagline: Drag two handles, trim your clip, done.

omakade.description: Omakade is a local-first game library for the Omarchy desktop that aggregates games you've installed across Steam, Lutris, Heroic, Faugus, RetroArch, Battle.net, Epic, GOG, and Amazon into a single cover-art browsing interface. It's built for keyboard and controller use, including a couch-mode layout, and stores everything locally rather than depending on a cloud service. It's an independent community project, not an official Omarchy app.
omakade.name: omakade

readme_screenshots.alt: Omakade library showing installed games from multiple launchers
Omakade game details showing playtime, IGDB insights, and Steam achievements

requirements: At least one supported game launcher (Steam, Lutris, Heroic, etc.) with installed games to display
omakade.tagline: One local game library that pulls together every launcher you use.

omapresent.description: Omapresent turns any plain Markdown file into a slide deck automatically, treating the structure of your writing as the deck itself. It runs a dual-window mode with a separate editor and audience display, supports speaker notes only you can see, auto-tiles consecutive images into grids, embeds videos, and can export the result as a PDF or a static web bundle. It picks up your Omarchy desktop theme's colors automatically.
omapresent.name: omapresent
requirements: Qt6 (base, declarative, webengine, webchannel, multimedia)
xdg-desktop-portal
omapresent.tagline: Write a Markdown file, get a presentation, no slide design required.

omarchy.description: Omarchy is a complete, ready-to-install Linux distribution built by DHH on top of Arch Linux and the Hyprland tiling window manager. Rather than making you assemble a desktop piece by piece, it ships with a curated terminal, Neovim setup, themes, hotkeys, and AI/agent tooling already configured and working together out of the box. It targets developers who want a fast, keyboard-centric, visually polished setup without doing the usual weeks of Arch ricing themselves.
omarchy.name: omarchy
omarchy.pricing_note: MIT licensed, free ISO download and install
requirements: A machine (or VM) that can run Arch Linux; installs as a full OS via ISO
omarchy.tagline: An opinionated Arch Linux desktop, pre-wired for keyboard-driven, agentic workflows.

omarchy-audio-tuner.description: Omarchy Audio Tuner is a command-line toolkit for authoring speaker tuning profiles that restore the vendor sound signature Linux normally strips away on laptops. It walks through capturing microphone measurements, analyzing frequency response, fitting a correction curve, and generating a PipeWire filter chain, with A/B auditioning to check the result. It's explicitly for advanced users building a tuning for a laptop model Omarchy doesn't already cover — most people never need it.
omarchy-audio-tuner.name: omarchy-audio-tuner
requirements: Python, FFmpeg, MPV, and LSP Plugins LV2 installed
A calibrated measurement microphone for building tunings from scratch (not required just to audition existing ones)
omarchy-audio-tuner.tagline: A measurement toolkit for building custom laptop-speaker EQ profiles on Linux.

omarchy-chromium.description: Omarchy Chromium was a fork of the Chromium web browser maintained specifically to give it live theme-switching support before upstream Chromium had that capability via policy-based refreshes. It behaved like a normal Chromium-based browser day to day, just with Omarchy's theme integration built in. The project has since been archived and marked read-only because the upstream Chromium project absorbed the underlying fix, making the fork unnecessary.
omarchy-chromium.name: omarchy-chromium
omarchy-chromium.tagline: A Chromium build patched for live theme switching on Omarchy.

omarchy-chromium-bin.description: Chromium is the open-source web browser project developed and used by Google as the base for Chrome, and also underlying Edge, Opera, Brave, and others. It aims to be a fast, safe, and stable way to browse the web, and its source and design documents are fully public. This package delivers a prebuilt Chromium binary with Omarchy's patches applied, so you get a working browser without compiling it yourself.
omarchy-chromium-bin.name: omarchy-chromium-bin
omarchy-chromium-bin.pricing_note: BSD-licensed source; site content under CC-BY 2.5
requirements: Network access to browse the web
omarchy-chromium-bin.tagline: Chromium, the open-source browser behind Chrome, packaged as a ready-to-run binary for Omarchy.

omarchy-dev.description: This is the same Omarchy Linux distribution by DHH, but built from the tip of its in-development 'quattro' branch rather than a stable release. It carries the same curated Hyprland desktop, terminal, editor, and agent tooling as the main omarchy package, just with the newest, potentially unstable changes applied first. It's meant for people who want to track Omarchy's development in real time rather than wait for tagged releases.
omarchy-dev.name: omarchy-dev
requirements: A machine (or VM) that can run Arch Linux
Tolerance for in-development, potentially unstable changes
omarchy-dev.tagline: The bleeding-edge development build of Omarchy, tracking the quattro branch tip.

omarchy-emacs.description: Omarchy Emacs is a small integration package that syncs Emacs to Omarchy's active theme and font automatically, so switching your system theme also restyles Emacs immediately, no restart needed. It pulls colors from Omarchy's generated theme file, reads the font family from Waybar's config, and reads the font size from whichever terminal (foot, Alacritty, kitty, or Ghostty) you have configured. It installs the Wayland-native build of Emacs for you as part of setup.
omarchy-emacs.name: omarchy-emacs
requirements: Arch Linux with Omarchy installed
emacs-wayland (installed automatically by the setup script)
One of foot, Alacritty, kitty, or Ghostty configured, for font-size detection
omarchy-emacs.tagline: Keeps Emacs looking and feeling like the rest of your Omarchy desktop, automatically.

omarchy-fish.description: Omarchy Fish is a configuration package that turns the Fish shell into a more productive out-of-the-box experience, adding custom functions, completions, and keybindings tuned for common developer tasks. It bundles fzf.fish for fuzzy-searching directories, git logs, shell history, and running processes, reachable through a set of Ctrl-based shortcuts. It also includes a small setup utility to make Fish your default shell.
omarchy-fish.name: omarchy-fish
requirements: Arch Linux
Fish shell
fzf.fish for the fuzzy-search functionality
omarchy-fish.tagline: A pre-built Fish shell setup with fuzzy search, git shortcuts, and Omarchy-friendly keybindings.

omarchy-herdr.description: Herdr is a background terminal runtime purpose-built for running AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor. It keeps each agent in its own real terminal session inside workspaces, tabs, and panes, and those sessions keep running even if you close the terminal or lose network — you reattach later with a single command. It shows at a glance which agents are working, blocked, or idle, and lets agents spawn panes or prompt each other for multi-agent coordination. This Omarchy package adds Omarchy-specific pane border styling on top of upstream Herdr.
omarchy-herdr.name: omarchy-herdr
requirements: A terminal — Herdr runs as a terminal-based runtime, not a standalone GUI app
omarchy-herdr.tagline: A persistent terminal runtime for keeping AI coding agents alive and organized in the background.

omarchy-keyring.description: Omarchy Keyring holds the PGP keys pacman uses to verify that Omarchy packages actually came from the Omarchy project and haven't been tampered with. It's a tiny, invisible piece of plumbing installed alongside the package manager configuration rather than something you interact with directly. Without it, pacman would refuse to trust signed Omarchy packages.
omarchy-keyring.name: omarchy-keyring
omarchy-keyring.tagline: The cryptographic keyring that lets pacman trust official Omarchy packages.

omarchy-nvim.description: Omarchy Neovim packages LazyVim, a popular configuration framework for the Neovim text editor, with its plugins pre-built and cached so you're not waiting on downloads and compilation the first time you open it. LazyVim turns plain Neovim into a full IDE-like environment: sensible default keybindings, file navigation, LSP support, and a large pre-configured plugin set, while still letting you customize anything. It's a terminal-based editor experience, not a separate graphical application.
omarchy-nvim.name: omarchy-nvim
requirements: Neovim 0.11.2+ (built with LuaJIT)
A C compiler (for nvim-treesitter)
A Nerd Font recommended for icons
omarchy-nvim.tagline: A ready-to-go LazyVim setup for Neovim, plugins pre-cached so it starts fast on first launch.

omarchy-settings.description: Omarchy-settings installs the baseline configuration for the Omarchy Linux distribution: the files that get copied into every new user's home directory (/etc/skel), the default font set, the Plymouth boot-splash theme, and small helper scripts the rest of the system relies on. It is not an app you open; it is the plumbing that makes a freshly installed Omarchy desktop look and behave consistently out of the box.
omarchy-settings.name: omarchy-settings
omarchy-settings.tagline: The default look, fonts, and boot theme Omarchy ships with, in one system package.

omarchy-settings-dev.description: This is a development build of omarchy-settings, pulling its defaults (skel files, fonts, Plymouth theme, helper scripts) from the tip of Omarchy's in-progress 'quattro' branch rather than a stable release. It exists so testers and contributors can run tomorrow's Omarchy defaults today, ahead of them landing in the main package.
omarchy-settings-dev.name: omarchy-settings-dev
requirements: Intended for users tracking Omarchy's development branch rather than a stable release; may be less tested than omarchy-settings
omarchy-settings-dev.tagline: The same Omarchy defaults package, built straight from the bleeding-edge quattro branch.

omarchy-walker.description: Omarchy-walker is a meta-package: it doesn't contain code itself but installs Walker, a fast GTK4/Rust application launcher for Wayland, together with Elephant, the provider system that feeds it results. Once installed, hitting the launcher keybind opens an overlay where you can search and launch apps, browse files, run calculations, look up symbols/emoji, search the clipboard, and more, all from one prefix-based search box.
omarchy-walker.name: omarchy-walker
omarchy-walker.tagline: Pulls in Walker, Omarchy's app launcher, wired up to search everything through Elephant.

omarchy-zsh.description: Omarchy-zsh applies Omarchy's system-wide shell configuration (aliases, functions, environment variables, pulled from the omadots dotfiles project) to Zsh, then layers on Zsh-specific extras like fzf-powered keybindings for fuzzy-searching files, command history, and git logs. Personal tweaks still go in your own ~/.zshrc, which is loaded on top and stays untouched by system updates.
omarchy-zsh.name: omarchy-zsh
omarchy-zsh.tagline: Turns Omarchy's shared shell config into a ready-to-use Zsh setup.

omasnap.description: Omasnap is a native screenshot and markup overlay for Hyprland on Wayland. Beyond capturing a region, window, or whole monitor, it lets you draw arrows, shapes, freehand lines, and text over the shot, blur or block out sensitive areas, run one-click OCR to pull text out of an image, and even stitch together scrolling captures of long pages. Finished screenshots can be pinned on top of your other windows or reopened later from a recent-captures shelf, with full undo history preserved even if the app crashes.
omasnap.name: omasnap
requirements: Wayland session with Hyprland (or a compositor offering equivalent window/monitor APIs)
omasnap.tagline: A tiny, fast Wayland screenshot tool that turns capture into a full annotation session.

omatrack.description: Omatrack is a desktop app for analyzing racing telemetry: it imports data from Pi/Cosworth, MoTeC, Racelogic, and AiM loggers and normalizes it all into one consistent per-lap model, so you can overlay traces, compare a lap against a reference lap, and step through corner-by-corner braking, turn-in, apex, and throttle data with synchronized onboard video. Sessions are organized by track, date, and session, and it can pull footage and logs straight from cloud storage (WebDAV, S3, Google Cloud Storage) instead of only local files.
omatrack.name: omatrack

readme_screenshots.alt: Omatrack comparison workspace with primary and reference telemetry traces
Omatrack corner analysis comparing braking, turn-in, apex, and throttle pickup

requirements: Telemetry/video files from a supported logger (Pi/Cosworth, MoTeC, Racelogic, or AiM) to have anything to analyze
omatrack.tagline: One workstation for reading, comparing, and picking apart motorsport telemetry from any data logger.

omawrite.description: Omawrite is a minimalist Markdown writing app built with Qt Quick, aimed at distraction-free drafting rather than full document editing. Markdown syntax stays visible but fades visually as you type, it follows your system's light or dark theme automatically, and it recovers unsaved drafts after a crash and warns you before an external edit would overwrite your work. It covers the basics newcomers expect: open/save/save-as through native file pickers, find and replace, and keyboard shortcuts for bold, italic, and links.
omawrite.name: omawrite
omawrite.tagline: A stripped-down Markdown editor that gets out of the way and just lets you write.

omazed.description: Omazed is a small Bash utility that watches for Omarchy theme changes and automatically regenerates a matching Zed editor theme, so switching your desktop's color palette also re-colors your code editor without any manual steps. After picking a theme once during setup, it keeps Zed synced through Omarchy's own theme-change hooks.
omazed.name: omazed
requirements: Omarchy (v3.8.0 or later) as the source of the color palette
Zed editor installed
omazed.tagline: Keeps your Zed editor theme in lockstep with whatever Omarchy color scheme you're running.
