once-bin.description: ONCE is a self-hosting platform from 37signals (Basecamp's parent company): a single Go binary that automates installing, updating, backing up, and monitoring Docker-based web applications on your own hardware, from a VPS down to a Raspberry Pi. It ships with 37signals' own apps ready to go but works with any Docker image that serves HTTP on port 80 and exposes a health-check endpoint, and it's driven through both a terminal dashboard and plain CLI commands.
once-bin.name: once-bin
requirements: A Docker-capable Linux or macOS machine to host apps on
Network access for pulling images, updates, and backups
once-bin.tagline: Turns any Linux or Mac machine into a self-hosted server for Docker web apps, with one install command.

openai-codex-bin.description: Codex CLI is OpenAI's lightweight AI coding agent that runs locally on your machine instead of in the cloud. From the terminal you describe what you want built, fixed, or explained, and it reads your codebase, edits files, and runs commands to get it done; it also plugs into editors like VS Code, Cursor, and Windsurf. It needs an OpenAI account to function, either signing in with a ChatGPT Plus/Pro/Business/Edu/Enterprise plan or authenticating with an OpenAI API key.
openai-codex-bin.name: openai-codex-bin
openai-codex-bin.pricing_note: CLI itself is free and open-source; using it requires a ChatGPT paid plan or pay-as-you-go OpenAI API usage
requirements: An OpenAI account: either a ChatGPT Plus/Pro/Business/Edu/Enterprise subscription, or an OpenAI API key with billing enabled
Network access to reach OpenAI's servers
openai-codex-bin.tagline: OpenAI's coding agent, living in your terminal and wired into your ChatGPT or API account.

openai-codex-desktop.description: The official ChatGPT desktop app bundled with Codex, OpenAI's agentic coding assistant. From one window you can chat with ChatGPT or hand a coding task to Codex, which can work across your local files and projects, run in cloud environments for longer jobs, and even do automatic code review. It's aimed at developers who want an agent that completes multi-step coding work rather than just answering questions.
openai-codex-desktop.name: openai-codex-desktop
openai-codex-desktop.pricing_note: Codex usage is included (limited) in the ChatGPT Free plan; expanded usage needs Go ($8/mo), Plus ($20/mo), Pro ($100-200/mo) or Business
requirements: A ChatGPT account
A paid ChatGPT plan (Plus, Pro, Business, etc.) for meaningful Codex usage beyond the free allowance
Network access
openai-codex-desktop.tagline: ChatGPT's desktop home for OpenAI's autonomous coding agent.
openai-codex-desktop.youtube_title: A research preview of Codex in ChatGPT

opencl-nvidia-580xx.description: This package provides the OpenCL implementation shipped with NVIDIA's 580xx proprietary driver series, so NVIDIA GPUs can be used for general-purpose parallel compute through the standard OpenCL API (alongside CUDA). It's a low-level driver component rather than an application — it does nothing on its own and is installed to pair with the matching nvidia-580xx driver package.
opencl-nvidia-580xx.name: opencl-nvidia-580xx
opencl-nvidia-580xx.pricing_note: Free driver component; requires owning NVIDIA hardware
requirements: An NVIDIA GPU supported by the 580xx driver branch
The matching nvidia-580xx driver package installed
opencl-nvidia-580xx.tagline: Lets NVIDIA GPUs crunch OpenCL workloads under the proprietary 580xx driver branch.

opencode.description: Opencode is an MIT-licensed, open-source coding agent centered on a rich terminal UI: you chat with it, it reads and edits files in your project, and runs commands on your behalf, with separate build (full-access) and plan (read-only) modes. A desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux is now available in beta on top of the same agent. You bring your own API key from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or any of 75+ supported providers.
opencode.name: opencode
opencode.pricing_note: The tool itself is free and open source; you pay your chosen LLM provider for API usage
requirements: An API key from a supported LLM provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, etc.) or a free/local model
Network access to the chosen provider
opencode.tagline: An open-source AI coding agent that lives in your terminal (and now a desktop app too).
opencode.youtube_title: OpenCode CRASH Course | OPEN SOURCE AI CODING AGENT

perplexity.description: The official desktop client for Perplexity, an AI answer engine that searches the web and returns a synthesized, source-cited response rather than just a list of results. The desktop app adds OS-level conveniences such as screenshot-to-search and quick access to chat and research directly from your desktop, on top of Perplexity's usual free and paid web features.
perplexity.name: perplexity
perplexity.pricing_note: Free plan available; Pro $20/mo, Max $50/mo, Enterprise $40/user/mo for advanced models and features
requirements: A Perplexity account (free or paid)
Network access
A paid subscription for advanced models, higher limits, and some premium features
perplexity.tagline: Perplexity's official desktop app for cited, AI-powered answers instead of a list of links.

pinta.description: Pinta is a free, open-source drawing and image-editing program for Linux, Mac, Windows and *BSD, modeled after the discontinued Paint.NET. It offers straightforward tools for freehand drawing, selection, cropping and resizing, over 35 real-time-preview effects and adjustments, layer support, and unlimited undo — aiming to be a simpler, more approachable alternative to heavyweight editors like GIMP for casual users.
pinta.name: pinta
pinta.tagline: A friendly, free painting and photo-editing app for people who find GIMP intimidating.
pinta.youtube_title: Pinta 2.0.1 - Drawing & Image Editor for Linux, macOS, & Windows Users

python-mediapipe.description: MediaPipe is a Google framework for building cross-platform, on-device machine learning pipelines — things like face, hand and pose detection, object tracking, and audio or text classification. It ships pre-trained models and cross-platform APIs (MediaPipe Tasks) so developers can add these ML features to mobile, web, and desktop apps without sending data to a server, along with tools to customize models on your own data.
python-mediapipe.name: python-mediapipe
python-mediapipe.tagline: Google's toolkit for running ready-made ML models for vision, audio and text right on-device.

python-sounddevice.description: python-sounddevice is a small Python library wrapping PortAudio, letting you play and record audio using NumPy arrays. It's aimed at developers, researchers and musicians who want simple, cross-platform programmatic control over audio input and output from Python, fitting naturally into existing NumPy-based signal-processing code.
python-sounddevice.name: python-sounddevice
requirements: The PortAudio library installed on the system
A working audio input/output device to actually record or play sound
python-sounddevice.tagline: Python bindings for PortAudio to record and play back sound as NumPy arrays.

python-terminaltexteffects.description: TerminalTextEffects (TTE) is a Python library and command-line tool that adds animated visual effects to text printed in the terminal — color gradients, particle-like motion paths, Matrix-style rain, and more. It ships 40+ built-in effects, usable either by piping text into the CLI application or by calling it as a library from your own scripts, with no third-party Python dependencies required.
python-terminaltexteffects.name: python-terminaltexteffects
requirements: A terminal that supports Xterm 256 or RGB hex colors
python-terminaltexteffects.tagline: A visual effects engine that animates terminal text output — think Matrix rain, but for any string.

qmk-hid.description: qmk_hid is a command-line tool from Framework Computer for controlling QMK-firmware keyboards through their raw HID interface (the same protocol VIA uses), without needing special drivers or admin rights on Windows or Linux. It can adjust RGB and backlight settings, read device info, jump into bootloader mode for firmware updates, and reset EEPROM/VIA settings. It works with any QMK device but was built and tested specifically for Framework's keyboard modules.
qmk-hid.name: qmk-hid
requirements: A QMK-firmware keyboard (developed and tested primarily on Framework Laptop 16 keyboard modules)
On Linux, udev rules installed to avoid needing root privileges
qmk-hid.tagline: A driver-free command-line tool for talking to QMK keyboards over raw HID.

quickshell-git.description: Quickshell is a flexible, code-first toolkit for building custom desktop shell components — status bars, widgets, lock screens, notification centers and more — using QtQuick/QML, primarily for Wayland compositors such as Hyprland (with X11 support too). Rather than a ready-made shell, it's a low-level building-block library with hot reloading that developers use to assemble their own desktop UI, so it powers other people's Hyprland setups rather than offering one out of the box.
quickshell-git.name: quickshell-git
requirements: Qt development libraries and a C++ toolchain to build from source
Programming in QML/C++ to actually build a shell with it — it is not a ready-made desktop UI
quickshell-git.tagline: A QtQuick-based toolkit for coding your own Linux desktop shell from scratch.

retroarch-joypad-autoconfig-git.description: A shared database of joypad autoconfig files for RetroArch, the multi-system emulator frontend. Each file maps a specific physical controller's buttons and sticks onto RetroArch's virtual RetroPad automatically, so gamepads are recognized and ready to use without manual button mapping. It's not an app on its own, just data that RetroArch reads on startup.
retroarch-joypad-autoconfig-git.name: retroarch-joypad-autoconfig-git
retroarch-joypad-autoconfig-git.tagline: Plug in a controller and RetroArch just knows what it is.

rog-control-center.description: ROG Control Center is the graphical front end for asusctl, the Linux control suite for ASUS ROG (and many other ASUS) laptops. It talks to the asusd background daemon over D-Bus to let you set keyboard RGB lighting and AniMe Matrix displays, tune per-profile fan curves, switch power/graphics modes, and manage battery charge limits, all from a windowed app instead of the command line.
rog-control-center.name: rog-control-center
rog-control-center.pricing_note: community-funded via Patreon/Ko-fi, no purchase needed
requirements: An ASUS ROG (or compatible ASUS) laptop with supported embedded controller hardware
The asusd daemon running in the background
A recent Linux kernel, since features track upstream kernel patches
rog-control-center.tagline: Windows-grade ROG laptop controls, built for the Linux desktop.

rustdesk.description: RustDesk is an open-source remote desktop app that lets you view and control another computer over the internet or a local network, similar to TeamViewer or AnyDesk. It works out of the box using RustDesk's public relay servers, or you can self-host your own rendezvous/relay server for full privacy and control. A paid RustDesk Server Pro edition adds enterprise features like address books, audit logs, and easier deployment for teams.
rustdesk.name: rustdesk
rustdesk.pricing_note: core app and self-hosted server free (AGPL-3.0); RustDesk Server Pro is a paid add-on for teams
requirements: Network access between the two machines (via RustDesk's relay or your own self-hosted server)
rustdesk.tagline: Your own TeamViewer, minus the subscription and the phone-home server.

schist.description: Schist is a layered image editor built in Rust with a plugin-first design, aimed at people who need real PSD and Affinity file compatibility on Linux without giving up source control. It ships dozens of brushes, selection and retouching tools, adjustment layers, and Photoshop-style filters, plus GPU-accelerated compositing, content-aware fill, liquify, and non-destructive editing. Every tool and filter is itself a plugin, so the whole editor is meant to be extended.
schist.name: schist
requirements: A Vulkan-capable GPU and driver for GPU-accelerated filters and compositing
schist.tagline: A Photoshop-fluent layered image editor that's actually open source.

schist-bin.description: Schist is a layered image editor built in Rust with a plugin-first design, aimed at people who need real PSD and Affinity file compatibility on Linux without giving up source control. It ships dozens of brushes, selection and retouching tools, adjustment layers, and Photoshop-style filters, plus GPU-accelerated compositing, content-aware fill, liquify, and non-destructive editing. This package installs the prebuilt binary release instead of compiling from source.
schist-bin.name: schist-bin
requirements: A Vulkan-capable GPU and driver for GPU-accelerated filters and compositing
schist-bin.tagline: A Photoshop-fluent layered image editor that's actually open source.

slap-notes-bin.description: Slap Notes is a local-first, block-based notes app that combines Notion-style blocks with Obsidian-style wiki-links, automatically building a visual graph of how your notes connect. It supports text, headings, lists, to-dos, tables, images and video blocks, daily notes, tagging, and full search. An optional built-in AI research agent can answer questions about your existing notes and draft new content back into your vault, but everything runs and stores locally otherwise.
slap-notes-bin.name: slap-notes-bin
slap-notes-bin.pricing_note: proprietary freeware, free to use and redistribute unmodified
requirements: Your own API key from a provider such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Groq, or OpenRouter, only if you want to use the optional AI research agent
slap-notes-bin.tagline: Notes that link to each other and can go do research for you.

spotify.description: Spotify is a proprietary music and podcast streaming service with a catalog of tens of millions of tracks. The free tier is ad-supported with shuffle-only play on mobile, while paid Premium plans remove ads and add offline downloads, unlimited skips, and on-demand playback. It requires a Spotify account and an internet connection to stream.
spotify.name: spotify
spotify.pricing_note: free ad-supported tier; Premium subscription for ad-free/offline listening
requirements: A Spotify account
Network access to stream
spotify.tagline: Millions of songs and podcasts, ad-free if you pay for it.

strata.description: Strata is a keyboard-first file manager for modern Linux desktops, built with GTK4 and designed to fit Omarchy-style setups. It offers three ways to browse, macOS-style Miller columns for spatial navigation, a thumbnail grid, and a sortable table view, along with instant fuzzy filename search, rich file previews, and sandboxed preview rendering for security.
strata.name: strata

readme_screenshots.alt: Strata Theme and appearance settings showing Omarchy following, six bundled themes, and the Add a theme option

requirements: GTK 4.12 or newer and a 64-bit Linux system with glibc 2.39+
strata.tagline: A file manager built for people who'd rather press keys than click.

sublime-text-4.description: Sublime Text is a proprietary text and code editor known for its speed, a distraction-free "Goto Anything" file/symbol jumper, multiple simultaneous cursors, and deep customization through plugins and key bindings. It can be downloaded and evaluated in full for free with no enforced time limit, but continued regular use is expected to be licensed.
sublime-text-4.name: sublime-text-4
sublime-text-4.pricing_note: $99 one-time personal license (includes 3 years of updates); free unlimited evaluation
sublime-text-4.tagline: The fast, endlessly customizable text editor that trusts you to pay for it.
sublime-text-4.youtube_title: [MG05] Introduction to the new features in Sublime Text 4!

sunshine.description: Sunshine is a self-hosted game stream host that works with the Moonlight client to let you play PC games remotely on another device, from a phone to a Steam Deck to a smart TV. It uses hardware encoding on AMD, Intel, or Nvidia GPUs when available, falling back to software encoding otherwise, and emulates Xbox, PlayStation, and Switch controllers for the client side.
sunshine.name: sunshine
requirements: A Moonlight client app on the device you'll stream to
A GPU with hardware encoding support (AMD, Intel, or Nvidia) for best performance, though software encoding works without one
Network access between the host and the streaming device
sunshine.tagline: Turn your own PC into a private game-streaming server.
sunshine.youtube_title: Setting up game streaming with Sunshine and Moonlight on Bazzite

supergfxctl.description: supergfxctl is a background daemon and command-line client for laptops that have both an integrated GPU and a discrete Nvidia GPU. It lets you flip between Hybrid, Integrated-only, VFIO passthrough, and ASUS-specific eGPU/MUX modes so you can trade battery life for graphics power on demand. It grew out of the ASUS ROG Linux tooling but works on other hybrid-graphics laptops too.
supergfxctl.name: supergfxctl
requirements: A laptop with hybrid integrated/discrete (Nvidia) graphics
A Wayland session (X11 switching is no longer supported)
On ASUS models, kernel 6.1 or newer
Not compatible with optimus-manager or system76-power installed alongside it
supergfxctl.tagline: Switch your laptop between integrated and discrete GPU modes without rebooting into a different OS setup.

symfony-cli.description: Symfony CLI is a terminal tool from the Symfony project that scaffolds new Symfony applications, runs a local development web server with HTTPS and Docker Compose integration, and handles day-to-day tasks like checking security advisories in your dependencies. It is aimed at PHP developers working with the Symfony framework and installs once as a single binary.
symfony-cli.name: symfony-cli
symfony-cli.tagline: The official command-line companion for building and running Symfony PHP applications.

t3code-bin.description: T3 Code is an open-source app that lets you monitor and steer multiple AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok, Antigravity) from a single desktop, web, or mobile interface. It connects to the coding-agent accounts you already pay for rather than reselling usage, and adds features like one-click GitHub pull-request creation with auto-generated titles and diff review.
t3code-bin.name: t3code-bin
t3code-bin.pricing_note: no token reselling or quota caps
requirements: Your own credentials/subscription for whichever coding agent(s) you connect (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.)
A GitHub account to use the pull-request features
t3code-bin.tagline: One control surface to drive Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other coding agents from your desktop or phone.
t3code-bin.youtube_title: So I tried Theo's T3 Code...

tensaku.description: Tensaku is a screenshot annotation app for Wayland desktops (Sway, Hyprland, and other wlroots-based compositors), forked from Satty. You take or paste a screenshot and add arrows, boxes, freehand marks, text callouts, and blur/redaction, with the twist that every annotation stays a movable, resizable object organized in a layers panel rather than being burned in immediately. It also supports stitching scrolling screenshots of tall content into one image.
tensaku.name: tensaku

readme_screenshots.alt: A screenshot annotated in Tensaku — arrows, colored text callouts, numbered markers, a highlight box, and a redaction blur

requirements: A wlroots-based Wayland compositor (Sway, Hyprland, River, Wayfire, etc.) that supports wlr-layer-shell and wlr-screencopy
tensaku.tagline: Mark up a screenshot with movable arrows, text, and blur, right from your Wayland compositor.

tmog-bin.description: TMOG (Task Manager OG) is a native system monitor and task manager built by Dave Plummer, the original author of Windows Task Manager, now rebuilt for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It shows CPU, GPU, memory, storage, network, power draw, and thermals alongside a process list and process tree, aiming for the depth and low overhead of a truly native app rather than a web-wrapped one.
tmog-bin.name: tmog-bin
tmog-bin.pricing_note: currently free beta; a paid Pro tier is planned but not yet on sale
tmog-bin.tagline: A dense, native task manager reborn: CPU, GPU, thermals, and processes at a glance, from the guy who wrote the original.
tmog-bin.youtube_title: TMOG: Dave Answers Your Questions + Rates 23 Feature Requests

tobi-try.description: try is a small command-line tool for people who spin up throwaway coding experiments constantly. Instead of hunting through a messy folder tree, you type a short name and it either fuzzy-jumps you into a matching, previously-created experiment directory or instantly creates a new date-prefixed one (like 2025-08-17-redis-experiment) and cds your shell into it. It can also clone a git repo straight into a new dated directory.
tobi-try.name: tobi-try
requirements: Ruby installed
Bash, Zsh, or Fish shell integration to enable the auto-cd behavior
tobi-try.tagline: Type a word, land in a fresh, dated folder for whatever idea you're chasing right now.

ttf-ia-writer.description: This package bundles iA Writer's own font families, iA Writer Mono, iA Writer Duo, and iA Writer Quattro, derived from IBM's Plex typeface family and tuned for distraction-free writing. They are the same fonts iA ships in its iA Writer apps across Mac, Windows, iOS, iPadOS, and Android, released here so anyone can install and use them system-wide.
ttf-ia-writer.name: ttf-ia-writer
ttf-ia-writer.pricing_note: SIL Open Font License; iA asks that forks credit iA Writer and not be used to clone its product or site
ttf-ia-writer.tagline: The clean monospaced and duo-width fonts behind the iA Writer app, free to use on your own desktop.

ttf-jetbrains-mono-nerd-basic.description: This is JetBrains' popular monospaced coding typeface run through the Nerd Fonts patcher, which adds glyphs from icon sets like Font Awesome, Devicons, and Octicons directly into the font. Terminal prompts, file-manager TUIs, and status bars that expect Nerd Font icon glyphs (folder icons, git branch symbols, language logos, and so on) render correctly once this font is installed and selected.
ttf-jetbrains-mono-nerd-basic.name: ttf-jetbrains-mono-nerd-basic
ttf-jetbrains-mono-nerd-basic.tagline: JetBrains Mono, patched with thousands of extra icons for terminals and code editors.

ttfx.description: ttfx is a single static binary that applies flashy visual effects, such as matrix-style rain, decryption reveals, fireworks, and waves, to text piped into it, for example `ls -la | ttfx decrypt`. It is a Rust rewrite of the Python TerminalTextEffects project, built for speed: it starts in under a millisecond and reportedly runs over 27 times faster than the original, so it is practical to drop into everyday shell pipelines rather than just for one-off demos.
ttfx.name: ttfx
requirements: A terminal that supports ANSI escape sequences
ttfx.tagline: Pipe any text through your terminal and watch it decrypt, burn, or rain down like The Matrix.

tuxedo-drivers-nocompatcheck-dkms.description: This package builds the same DKMS kernel modules TUXEDO Computers ships for its laptops, covering function keys, keyboard backlight, fan control, power profiles, and other embedded-controller sensors, but with the hardware compatibility check disabled. That lets it run on laptops from other brands that share the same underlying barebone hardware as a supported TUXEDO model (for example a TUXEDO Pulse 14 Gen 4 and a rebadged Schenker Via 14 Pro). The maintainer warns this bypass can be risky since embedded-controller code that targets the wrong hardware can potentially cause damage.
tuxedo-drivers-nocompatcheck-dkms.name: tuxedo-drivers-nocompatcheck-dkms
requirements: A laptop whose hardware is identical or near-identical to a model TUXEDO's drivers already support (e.g. NB05/NB04/NB02, Sirius 16, or a rebadged equivalent from another brand)
DKMS and kernel headers for the running kernel
tuxedo-drivers-nocompatcheck-dkms.tagline: TUXEDO's laptop kernel drivers, with the model whitelist switched off so lookalike laptops can use them too.

typora.description: Typora merges the writing and preview panes into one live document: type an asterisk for bold or a hash for a heading and it renders instantly, with no separate preview window and no visible syntax clutter. It handles tables, code blocks, math, diagrams, and images inline, and can export a finished document to PDF, Word, LaTeX, EPUB, and other formats. Outline navigation, focus/typewriter modes, and CSS-based theming round it out for long-form writing.
typora.name: typora
typora.pricing_note: $14.99 one-time, licensed for up to 3 devices; 15-day free trial
requirements: Purchases a license after the 15-day trial to keep using it
typora.tagline: Markdown that never asks you to look at markdown.

tzupdate.description: tzupdate is a small command-line tool that figures out your timezone by looking up your public IP address against geolocation services, then updates the system timezone automatically. It's meant for machines that move around, or for skipping manual timezone setup entirely. A preview flag lets you see the detected timezone before it changes anything.
tzupdate.name: tzupdate
requirements: Network access to reach IP geolocation services
Root/administrator privileges to change the system timezone
tzupdate.tagline: Your clock, wherever your IP address says you are.

ufw-docker.description: By default, Docker writes its own iptables rules that bypass UFW, so a published container port can be reachable from the internet even though UFW looks like it's blocking it. ufw-docker patches UFW's rule files so container ports are only exposed the way you explicitly allow with normal `ufw route allow` commands, while still letting containers talk to each other internally.
ufw-docker.name: ufw-docker
requirements: Docker and UFW already installed
Root/sudo access to edit /etc/ufw/after.rules
ufw-docker.tagline: Closes the hole Docker punches through your firewall.

umu-launcher.description: umu-launcher packages Valve's Proton compatibility tooling and the Steam Linux Runtime so any launcher, not just Steam, can run Windows games on Linux. Tools like Lutris, Heroic, and Bottles use it under the hood to set up the Wine prefix, pick a Proton version, and apply community game-specific fixes automatically.
umu-launcher.name: umu-launcher
requirements: A Proton or Proton-compatible build to actually run games
Network access to download the Steam Runtime and game-fix database on first run
umu-launcher.tagline: Proton for your Windows games, no Steam required.

v4l2-relayd.description: v4l2-relayd is a small background service that uses GStreamer to relay a video source, a file, a network stream, or another camera, into a v4l2loopback virtual camera device. Once running, other applications (video calls, streaming software) can pick the virtual device up as if it were a regular webcam.
v4l2-relayd.name: v4l2-relayd
requirements: v4l2loopback kernel module loaded
GStreamer installed
v4l2-relayd.tagline: Pipes any video source into a virtual webcam device.

visual-studio-code-bin.description: Visual Studio Code is a free code editor from Microsoft with built-in debugging, Git integration, an integrated terminal, and IntelliSense completions, extendable through a marketplace of tens of thousands of extensions covering nearly every language and framework. Recent versions add AI coding agents that can plan and carry out multi-step edits, run commands, and iterate, on top of the traditional editing experience.
visual-studio-code-bin.name: visual-studio-code-bin
visual-studio-code-bin.pricing_note: Free binary; Microsoft's own build under a proprietary (non-OSS) license, distinct from the open-source Code - OSS project
requirements: A GitHub account to use the built-in AI agent features
visual-studio-code-bin.tagline: The code editor most developers open first.
visual-studio-code-bin.youtube_title: Learn Visual Studio Code in 15 minutes: 2026 Official Beginner Tutorial

voxtype-bin.description: Voxtype turns speech into typed text: hold a push-to-talk hotkey, speak, and release, and the transcription is typed at your cursor or copied to the clipboard. Transcription runs locally through engines like Whisper or Parakeet rather than a cloud service, and it can automatically duck your music while you're dictating. It works across GNOME, KDE, Sway, Hyprland, and River.
voxtype-bin.name: voxtype-bin
requirements: Optional GPU (NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm/MIGraphX, or Vulkan) to accelerate transcription; runs on CPU otherwise
voxtype-bin.tagline: Hold a key, talk, get text, all on-device.

walker.description: Walker is a fast, GTK4-based application launcher for Linux that goes beyond opening apps: type a prefix to do quick math, browse files, run shell commands, search the web, dig through clipboard history, or manage Arch packages, all from the same popup. It's built for tiling Wayland setups like Hyprland and is themed and configured through simple config files.
walker.name: walker
requirements: Its companion 'Elephant' service running in the background
walker.tagline: One popup for apps, math, files, and more.
walker.youtube_title: Setup WALKER, the Application Launcher. A Step-by-Step Guide from Installation, Theming to Scripting

wayfreeze.description: wayfreeze is a tiny utility for Wayland compositors that freezes what's currently on screen, a still frame you can then screenshot or annotate without anything shifting underneath you. It supports multiple monitors, fractional scaling, and can hide the cursor or run commands before and after the freeze.
wayfreeze.name: wayfreeze
requirements: A wlroots-based compositor supporting the wlr-layer-shell, wlr-screencopy, wp-fractional-scale, and wp-viewporter protocols
wayfreeze.tagline: Pauses your screen so you can screenshot it in peace.

xdg-terminal-exec.description: xdg-terminal-exec is a reference implementation of a proposed freedesktop.org standard for launching a user's preferred terminal emulator, the same way xdg-open resolves a preferred browser or file handler. Instead of a script or app hard-coding a specific terminal, it calls xdg-terminal-exec and the system resolves whichever terminal the user has configured, optionally running a command inside it.
xdg-terminal-exec.name: xdg-terminal-exec
requirements: Terminal emulators need a compatible desktop entry (TerminalEmulator category with an X-TerminalArgExec key) to be selectable
xdg-terminal-exec.tagline: Lets apps open 'the terminal' without guessing which one.

xpadneo-dkms.description: xpadneo is a kernel driver that lets Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S, and Xbox Elite Series 2 wireless controllers connect to Linux over Bluetooth with full feature support, not just basic button input. It adds rumble, proportional trigger feedback, battery-level reporting, and paddle button support that the generic in-kernel driver lacks. It started as a student project at fortiss GmbH (affiliated with TU Munich) and is packaged here via DKMS so the kernel module rebuilds automatically across kernel updates.
xpadneo-dkms.name: xpadneo-dkms
requirements: A Bluetooth adapter (Bluetooth Low Energy support needed for Xbox Series X|S controllers)
An Xbox wireless controller (One S, Series X|S, or Elite Series 2) to pair
xpadneo-dkms.tagline: Makes your Xbox wireless controller feel first-class on Linux, over Bluetooth.

yaru-gnome-shell-theme.description: This package installs the GNOME Shell portion of Yaru, Ubuntu's default desktop theme, styling the top bar, overview, lock screen, and system menus to match Ubuntu's look. It's derived from the official upstream GNOME Shell theme and ships in light and dark variants. Installing it alone gives you Yaru's shell styling without pulling in the full icon or GTK theme.
yaru-gnome-shell-theme.name: yaru-gnome-shell-theme
yaru-gnome-shell-theme.tagline: Ubuntu's signature look, for the GNOME Shell chrome around your desktop.

yaru-gtk-theme.description: This is the core GTK2/GTK3 stylesheet of Yaru, Ubuntu's default theme, controlling how buttons, menus, title bars, and other widgets look and feel across GTK applications. It's built on top of upstream Adwaita and ships light and dark variants. This is the largest and most visible piece of the Yaru suite since it affects nearly every application window.
yaru-gtk-theme.name: yaru-gtk-theme
yaru-gtk-theme.tagline: The GTK widget theme behind Ubuntu's familiar desktop look.

yaru-gtksourceview-theme.description: This package provides a GtkSourceView color scheme matching the Yaru theme, so code editors and text views built on the GtkSourceView library (like GNOME Text Editor or gedit) get syntax highlighting that fits the rest of the Yaru-themed desktop. It's a small, focused piece of the wider Yaru theme suite.
yaru-gtksourceview-theme.name: yaru-gtksourceview-theme
yaru-gtksourceview-theme.tagline: Ubuntu-matching syntax highlighting colors for GTK-based text and code views.

yaru-icon-theme.description: Yaru's icon theme provides application, folder, and system icons for the Ubuntu desktop, built from the Unity8 Suru icon set and its Suru successor. It's the component most people recognize as 'the Ubuntu look' — orange folder icons, flat colorful app icons, and a matching cursor theme. It's the largest Yaru sub-package by size since it bundles a large set of icon assets.
yaru-icon-theme.name: yaru-icon-theme
yaru-icon-theme.tagline: The colorful, rounded icon set that defines Ubuntu's visual identity.

yaru-metacity-theme.description: This package brings Yaru's visual style to Metacity, the window manager used in GNOME Flashback and some classic desktop setups, theming window borders, title bars, and controls to match the rest of the Yaru suite. It's a small, targeted component for users running a Metacity-based session rather than modern GNOME Shell.
yaru-metacity-theme.name: yaru-metacity-theme
yaru-metacity-theme.tagline: Ubuntu-styled window borders and decorations for the Metacity window manager.

yaru-session.description: This is a tiny metadata package that registers Yaru as a coherent desktop session/theme option, tying together the GTK, icon, shell, and sound components so a display manager or settings panel can offer 'Yaru' as a single selectable theme. It contains no visual assets itself.
yaru-session.name: yaru-session
yaru-session.tagline: The glue package that wires Yaru up as a selectable desktop session.

yaru-sound-theme.description: This package provides Yaru's system sound theme, the audio cues for logging in, notifications, alerts, and other desktop events. It combines sounds from the WoodenBeaver and Touch-Remix projects into one cohesive set matching Ubuntu's default sound design.
yaru-sound-theme.name: yaru-sound-theme
yaru-sound-theme.tagline: The login, notification, and alert sounds that come with Ubuntu.

yaru-unity-theme.description: This package adapts the Yaru theme for the Unity desktop environment, styling Unity's launcher, top panel, and dash to match the rest of the Yaru suite. It's aimed at users still running or reviving a Unity session rather than modern GNOME Shell.
yaru-unity-theme.name: yaru-unity-theme
yaru-unity-theme.tagline: Yaru's styling for the Unity desktop's launcher and panel.

yaru-xfwm4-theme.description: This package themes xfwm4, the window manager used by Xfce, with Yaru's window borders, title bars, and decorations so an Xfce session can visually match the rest of the Yaru desktop suite. It's for users pairing Xfce with Ubuntu's default theming rather than GNOME.
yaru-xfwm4-theme.name: yaru-xfwm4-theme
yaru-xfwm4-theme.tagline: Ubuntu's Yaru look, brought to the Xfce window manager.

yay.description: yay is a command-line helper for Arch Linux that wraps pacman and adds support for the Arch User Repository (AUR). It resolves dependencies, downloads and lets you review PKGBUILDs before building, searches both official repos and the AUR in one command, and can track and update development (-git) packages. It's the de facto standard way Arch and Arch-based distros like Omarchy install community packages that aren't in the official repositories.
yay.name: yay
requirements: An AUR account (username/password via env vars) only if you want to use its package-voting feature; not needed for normal install/search/update use
yay.tagline: The AUR helper that makes pacman feel complete.

yt6801-dkms.description: This package is a DKMS-packaged kernel module for the Motorcomm YT6801, a Gigabit PCIe Ethernet controller chip found in some laptop and desktop motherboards (including certain models this driver was added to Omarchy for). DKMS means the module is automatically rebuilt whenever your kernel updates, so wired networking keeps working across kernel upgrades without manual recompilation. It has no user interface; it just needs to be installed on a machine that actually has this specific ethernet chip.
yt6801-dkms.name: yt6801-dkms
requirements: Only useful on hardware that actually has a Motorcomm YT6801 Gigabit PCIe Ethernet controller chip
Linux kernel headers installed for DKMS to build against
yt6801-dkms.tagline: The Linux driver that lets a Motorcomm YT6801 chip actually talk to your network.
